text.en: A short poem wonders where the bright Sun goes at night. It sinks behind a faraway hill, the world grows dark and quiet, and the child sleeps until morning, when the Sun is shining again. In this chapter you will read the poem, think about day and night, play I Spy, practise the sounds sp, st and sk, and make new words with sun.

The poem asks a simple question: where does the bright Sun go at night? In the poem, the Sun seems to slip behind a distant hill. The place where the child lives grows dark and quiet. The child goes to bed and sleeps until the day begins to peep, which means to show a little. When the child opens their eyes in the morning, the Sun is shining again. So the poem shows the whole day and night in a few lines, from sunset to sunrise.
Day and night happen because the Earth turns. The side facing the Sun has daylight. The Sun keeps shining while our side turns away. When our side turns away from the Sun, it is night for us, and when it turns back, it is morning again. Plants, flowers, children and animals all need the Sun, because its light and warmth help them grow and stay healthy. A sunflower and plants need sunlight to make their food. A table and toys do not need the Sun to live.
At sunrise and sunset the sky shows orange, red, pink and yellow. In the night sky we can see the Moon and many stars. During the day we see the Sun, clouds and birds. When you open your eyes in the morning you may feel fresh and happy, because a new day has begun.
To wonder is to think about something and want to know about it. Distant means far away. Peep means to look or appear for a short time.
Some words start with two consonant sounds that come one after another. We say them together in a blend, and both sounds are still there. Sp words are spy, spin, spoon and splash. St words are star, storm, store, stick, stair and stain. Sk words are sky, skin and skate. Say each word slowly and listen to how it starts. I spy a few stars in the sky has all three sounds.
We can add sun to other words to make new words. Sun and light make sunlight. Sun and flower make sunflower. Sun and beam make sunbeam. Sun and set make sunset, sun and rise make sunrise, sun and glasses make sunglasses, and sun and day make Sunday. Each of these is a compound word, made by joining two small words.
One child is the Spy and secretly chooses something in the room. The Spy says I spy with my little eye something that is blue, and gives a clue. Everyone looks around and guesses. If it is tricky, the Spy gives more clues. The child who guesses right becomes the next Spy.

Imagine a torch shining on a ball. Put a small paper dot on the ball to mark a home. Which part of the ball is lit?

board.text: Torch → lit side of the ball

text.en: Keep the torch still and slowly turn the ball. When the dot moves into shade, it is night for that home. When it returns to the lit side, it is day there.

board.text: Turn the ball: day → night → day

text.en: Say spin, stop and skip. Each starts with an s sound. Listen for the sound that comes next: p in spin, t in stop and k in skip.

board.text: spin: sp | stop: st | skip: sk

text.en: Make two word cards, sun and rise. Put them together and say sunrise. Now swap rise for set and explain what changes in the meaning.
For I Spy, give two clues about something you can see. Try naming its colour and telling where it is. Let your partner guess and explain which clue helped.

text.en: Join the two small words.
Sun and set make sunset.
